note: The judges saw only the advisory text and the finding text, with opaque ids and an order fixed by a hash unrelated to the arm. The arm and the original id are joined back in here, afterwards, from the mapping file they never received.

judgements.reason: Mechanism is an if-condition string comparison in the boot script where two failed sha256sum redirects both yield '' and compare equal, so a stale guest-agent binary is misreported as up-to-date. That is an update-integrity defect in a different file, with no bearing on who may connect to /run/lima-guestagent.sock. The finding itself states no attacker-controlled path exists.

Mechanism is a root chown without --no-dereference on a mount point that may be a symlink, in the cidata boot script. The consequence (ownership of an attacker-chosen directory transferred to the lima uid) and the place are unrelated to the guest agent socket's permissions or the tunnelling service the advisory is about.

Mechanism is `eval echo $VAR` performing glob expansion and word splitting on the mount-point value before root's mkdir/chown, in the boot script. Different file, different mechanism (shell expansion steering a chown target) and different consequence from the world-accessible guest agent socket.

Mechanism is an unescaped sed transform of lima.env into /etc/conf.d/lima-guestagent, where a value containing a quote plus $(...) executes as root when OpenRC sources the file. The trust boundary crossed is host config -> guest root, not local guest user -> root via the agent socket; different file and different mechanism.

Exactly the advisory's defect: os.Chmod(socket, 0o777) on /run/lima-guestagent.sock in daemon_linux.go plus no peer-credential check between Accept and server.StartServer, so any local guest uid drives the root daemon's API including the port-forwarding tunnel server. Same place, same mechanism, same consequence (non-root guest principal acting through a root process).

Mechanism is a root `rm -f` in the boot script resolving symlinks in intermediate path components under the guest user's home, redirecting one unlink of a fixed filename. Different file, different mechanism, and a bounded deletion primitive rather than access to the guest agent socket.

Same defect: the hardcoded /run/lima-guestagent.sock is chmod 0o777 at daemon_linux.go:141 while the daemon runs as uid 0, and no SO_PEERCRED or other gate exists before the GuestServer/TunnelServer is served, so any local guest uid reaches the root RPC surface. The finding hedges only on the maximum blast radius, which the advisory's severity question does not affect.

Mechanism is unvalidated interpolation of --virtio-port (and the binary path) into the systemd unit template and into a /dev/virtio-ports path concatenation. Different file, host-side config as the input, and the consequence is unit injection / path traversal, not local guest access to the agent socket.

Same file and the same general concern (who may reach the root guest agent's server), but a different mechanism: a fail-open type assertion in cidFilteredListener.Accept on the vsock transport, not the 0777 UNIX socket. The advisory states the vsock/vz path is not exploitable, and the finding concedes triggerability is undetermined.
judgements.what_would_settle_it: Whether the v2.1.3 patch changed cidFilteredListener's assertion structure as part of this fix, or only the UNIX socket's permissions/ownership.

judgements.reason: Same file and same access-control surface, different mechanism and consequence: the nested type assertions in the vsock CID filter default to allow. The finding explicitly claims no exploit path and says the rule holds as written today, so it does not describe the world-writable UNIX socket the advisory is about.
judgements.what_would_settle_it: Whether the patch touched the vsock filter's default-deny shape rather than only the UNIX socket permissions.

judgements.reason: Same file and same trust boundary in the abstract (a local guest process reaching the root agent), but the mechanism is a hypothetical fail-open of the vsock host-CID filter when Accept returns an unexpected concrete type - conditional on a dependency change - not the chmod 0777 on the UNIX socket that the advisory identifies as the exploitable defect on the qemu driver.
judgements.what_would_settle_it: Whether the fix commit altered cidFilteredListener.Accept to deny by default, or only hardened the UNIX socket path.

judgements.reason: The advisory's defect precisely: daemon_linux.go:141 chmod 0o777 on /run/lima-guestagent.sock served by a uid-0 daemon with no authentication, letting any local guest user speak the gRPC API and drive the port-forwarding TunnelServer - the same tunnelling-to-arbitrary-address capability the advisory says yields root in the VM.

Mechanism is the '' = '' comparison when both sha256sum reads fail in the boot script, so a missing/unreadable cidata image is reported as up-to-date and the install is skipped. An integrity/verification defect in a different file; nothing to do with socket permissions or the tunnelling service.

Mechanism is the symlink-following root chown of mount points in the boot script (no -h, no [ -L ] test), letting a planted link move ownership of a chosen directory to the lima uid. Different file, different mechanism; the escalation route runs through the lima user's sudo, not through the guest agent socket.

Same symlink-dereferencing root chown of the reverse-sshfs mount point in the boot script as P-008/P-070. Different file and different mechanism from the world-accessible guest agent socket; only the coarse outcome (local user -> root in guest) coincides, which is not enough.

Describes cookie precedence: the bare <Name> cookie returned inside the loop at :114-115 wins over accumulated multipart parts, so authorization runs on a superseded token. That is a session-integrity defect on the read path, not the unbounded make([]string, numParts) allocation the advisory is about; it neither reaches nor depends on the allocation line, and the consequence (stale/overridden session) has nothing to do with process OOM.

Sensitive-data-in-logs: cookie.Value and the reassembled token written to log.Debugw at :119-122 and :146-148. Different mechanism (no redaction of a credential) and different consequence (credential replay by log readers) from the attacker-controlled slice length causing fatal OOM.

Points at the advisory's exact statement (:126, strconv.Atoi(xyArray[1])) but names a different defect in it: the missing length check on the strings.Split result, giving an index-out-of-range panic when the name has no 'of'. The advisory's defect is the missing upper bound on the parsed value that feeds make([]string, N). Different mechanism (slice index vs allocation size) and different consequence (recoverable per-request panic / lockout vs unrecoverable runtime OOM killing the process).

Same reassembly block, but the defect asserted is unvalidated part INDEXES: xyArray[1] read without a length check (:126) and cookieParts[i-1] written without checking 1 <= i <= numParts (:136), producing index-out-of-range panics plus a no-attacker stale-part case. It never claims the parsed count is unbounded or that allocation size is the problem; consequence is a per-request panic, not a fatal out-of-memory process kill.

A write-path sizing defect in setCookie: the chunk budget at :73 is computed from the base cookie name while parts are emitted with a longer '_XofY' name (:76), so each part overshoots the 4000-byte target. Different function, different mechanism, and the consequence is dropped parts / redirect loops, not attacker-driven allocation.

Cites the advisory's numParts latch at :125-130 but only as context for a different defect: cookieParts[i-1] at :136 with i from xyArray[0] and no range test, so consistent-looking names like '_1of2' then '_3of9' overrun the slice. The exploitable element is the unchecked index, not the unbounded allocation size, and the consequence is a recoverable panic rather than a fatal OOM.

Exactly the advisory's defect: numParts parsed from the client-controlled cookie name at :126 with no bound and passed straight to make([]string, numParts) at :130, so one Cookie header (_1of2000000000) forces a multi-gigabyte allocation and kills the unauthenticated-reachable proxy. Same mechanism, same lines, same consequence.

splitCookie (:201-212) with a non-positive maxLen derived from the :73 budget: negative index or a non-advancing append loop. Write path, operator/configuration-triggered, and the input is the configured cookie name/domain rather than a request-supplied part count. Different defect from the request-driven unbounded make().

The advisory's defect stated precisely: the cookie name selects the allocation size at make([]string, numParts) (:130) via the unbounded Atoi at :126, landing in the band that reaches mallocgc and Go's unrecoverable 'fatal error: out of memory', which net/http's per-connection recover cannot catch. Same mechanism, same place, same process-death consequence.

ClearCookie (:165-174) omits the SameSite attribute that setCookie writes, so under sameSite=none the deletion cookie is rejected cross-site and logout does not remove the session. Different function, different mechanism (attribute drift between set and clear paths), different consequence (session survives logout).

splitCookie's backward UTF-8 walk at :206 with no lower bound and a chunk loop that can fail to advance. Cookie-writing path, driven by the configured size budget rather than a client-supplied part count; the finding itself states reachability from request input is unproven. Different defect from the reassembly allocation.

ClearCookie's HasPrefix on the bare configured name at :163 deletes co-hosted applications' cookies on logout. Different function, different mechanism (over-broad prefix match on the delete path), different consequence (collateral cookie deletion). The passing reference to :126 is context, not the claimed defect.

Same SameSite-omission-on-logout defect in ClearCookie (:165-174) as P-031/P-046: attribute drift between the set and clear paths, consequence is a surviving session cookie after logout. Unrelated to the multipart count driving make().

ClearCookie's deletion cookie takes SameSite(0) so the attribute is omitted and browsers treat it as Lax, breaking logout in sameSite=none deployments. Different function, mechanism and consequence from the unbounded multipart allocation.

Sits in the same reassembly logic and cites the advisory's make([]string, numParts) at :130, but the asserted defect is the absence of any completeness/consistency check before the join at :141: holes, duplicate indexes and orphaned parts are silently returned as a valid token. The advisory's exploitable element is the size of that allocation; here the allocation is only the source of zero-filled holes. Different mechanism, different consequence (silent token corruption).
Cleartext logging of the session JWT at :119-122 and :146-148. Credential disclosure through the log pipeline, not the attacker-controlled slice allocation; nothing in it touches numParts or make().

ClearCookie emits deletions only from inside the loop over cookies the request carried (:162-163) and has no return value, so a logout with no matching cookie silently deletes nothing. Different function, mechanism and consequence.

The same write-path budget overrun as P-014: chunk size measured with the base name at :64-73 while parts are renamed with a '_%dof%d' suffix at :76, so each part is a few bytes over the 4000-byte budget. The finding explicitly says it is not exploitable. Unrelated to the request-driven allocation.

Same function and the same client-controlled name, but the defect is the unchecked slice WRITE at :136 (cookieParts[i-1] with no 1 <= i <= numParts test), giving index-out-of-range panics from _9of1 or _0of1. The advisory's defect is the unchecked allocation SIZE at :130; the finding treats numParts as merely latched, never as unbounded. Consequence is a per-request 500 that net/http recovers, not the fatal OOM.
Session token written to the log in clear text on the read path (:119-122, :146-148). Credential exposure via log sinks; different mechanism and consequence from the multipart allocation DoS.

The advisory's defect: numParts from strconv.Atoi(xyArray[1]) at :126, derived purely from cookie.Name, passed with no upper bound, no lower bound and no cross-check to make([]string, numParts) at :130, so an unauthenticated request header drives an arbitrarily large allocation up to fatal 'runtime: out of memory' that kills the auth service. Same mechanism, same lines, same consequence.

Same statement as the advisory (:126) but the missing check it names is the length of the strings.Split result, not the magnitude of the parsed count: 'VouchCookie_x' yields a one-element slice and indexing xyArray[1] panics before Atoi ever runs. Different mechanism (bad index vs unbounded allocation) and different consequence (recoverable 500 per request vs unrecoverable process-killing OOM).

Same general area (the unauthenticated payment-webhook route block, line 61 vs the advisory's lines 56-58) but a different route and a different mechanism: environment selection from an attacker-controlled :env path segment leading to signature/secret confusion and paid-balance forgery. The advisory's defect is unbounded body read plus full-body logging before signature validation, and it explicitly states forgery was NOT possible because signature validation still guarded processing.

Process-wide TLS certificate validation disabled by mutating http.DefaultTransport in common/init.go. Different file, different mechanism (MITM on outbound HTTPS), different consequence (identity-provider impersonation / account takeover). Nothing to do with webhook request-body handling.
Trusted-redirect-domain allowlist parsed without hostname validation -> open redirect / OAuth code smuggling. Unrelated mechanism and consequence.
Missing SecureVerificationRequired step-up on the token-key route. Authorization gap on an authenticated route; not the unauthenticated webhook body-read DoS.
Account-binding OAuth routes registered without UserAuth -> account-takeover primitive. Different routes, different mechanism, different consequence.
NODE_TYPE role selection fails open to master -> duplicated billing/quota jobs. Different file and a financial-integrity defect, not the webhook DoS.

Unauthenticated POST /api/setup lacking CriticalRateLimit and TurnstileCheck -> privilege bootstrap. Different endpoint and a privilege-escalation consequence; says nothing about unbounded body reads or pre-validation logging.
Auth-factor removal and account deletion routes require only a session (no step-up, no critical rate limit). Authenticated-session abuse, unrelated to the advisory's defect.
Logout exposed as a state-changing GET with no anti-CSRF gate. Different route, CSRF mechanism, session-denial consequence.
Token key disclosure endpoints missing step-up verification -> credential exfiltration from a hijacked session. Different mechanism and consequence.
Unauthenticated /api/ratio_config discloses pricing config, bypassing the pricing module gate. Information disclosure on a different route.
GetUserGroups mounted a second time without auth. Missing-authentication/disclosure defect on a user route, not the payment-webhook body handling.
Same duplicate anonymous GetUserGroups mount; reconnaissance disclosure of billing tiers. Different defect entirely.

DIFY_DEBUG defaults to true -> verbose relay logging of prompts and upstream keys. It shares the word 'logging' with the advisory, but the mechanism is a debug default in common/init.go on the authenticated relay path and the consequence is sensitive-data disclosure, not unauthenticated memory/disk exhaustion via oversized webhook bodies.
Gemini/Cohere safety filters default to off. Content-policy exposure in a config initializer; no relation to the webhook defect.
Same upstream safety-filter defaults defect. Unrelated to unauthenticated webhook body processing.
CountToken read from a camelCase env name so the option is silently ignored. Configuration/billing correctness defect; unrelated.
Logout as a state-changing GET without CSRF protection. Different route, mechanism and consequence.
NODE_TYPE fail-open to master node. Different file and defect class.
CryptoSecret silently derived from SESSION_SECRET with no validation of an unset value. Key-management defect leading to cookie forgery and at-rest decryption; unrelated to the webhook body defect.

Log directory created with mode 0777 (plus os.Mkdir only creating the leaf). Touches logs, but the mechanism is filesystem permissions and the consequence is local tampering/reading of log files - not unbounded full-body logging of unauthenticated requests filling the disk.
Group-wide gzip over /api including credential-returning responses (BREACH side channel). Different mechanism and consequence, even though the middleware chain overlaps the webhook routes.
Anonymous duplicate mount of GetUserGroups. Missing-auth disclosure on a user route; different defect.
State-changing operations bound to GET (token generation, logout, admin channel sweeps) -> CSRF/prefetch triggering. Different mechanism and consequence.
Bulk channel-key management gated only by AdminAuth while single-key read requires root plus step-up. Authorization-tier inconsistency; unrelated.

DIFY_DEBUG defaulting to enabled -> verbose relay logging into the 0777 log directory. The 'logging' overlap is superficial: a boot-time debug default on the relay path with a disclosure consequence, not pre-signature-validation full-body logging of anonymous webhook requests causing DoS.

Unauthenticated GET/POST /api/setup missing CriticalRateLimit and TurnstileCheck -> automated racing of the administrator-provisioning route. It enumerates the /api group middleware (including BodyStorageCleanup) but only to argue that the setup pair lacks anti-automation gates; the defect is privilege bootstrap on a different endpoint, not unbounded body reads or pre-validation logging on payment webhooks.

Points at the advisory's exact endpoints (it names the webhooks on lines 56-58 as unrate-limited) but as one part of a broader claim about all payment notification callbacks, and the mechanism it argues is different: GET registration leaking signatures into query-string logs plus absent CriticalRateLimit enabling signature hammering with a DB lookup per attempt. It never describes the unbounded body read or the full-body logging before signature validation, and its consequence is signature abuse/log leakage rather than memory pressure and disk growth.
judgements.what_would_settle_it: Whether the finding anywhere ties the missing limit to request BODY size read before validation, rather than to request count.

judgements.reason: TLS_INSECURE_SKIP_VERIFY mutating the process-global transport. Different file, MITM mechanism, confidentiality/integrity consequence.

Names the advisory's webhook registrations (lines 56-58) among a broader set of unauthenticated payment callbacks, but the asserted mechanism is absent rate limiting plus GET binding plus an :env selector that may fail open, with consequences of signature brute force, replay, double-crediting and credit forgery. The advisory's defect - reading and logging the whole body before signature validation, fixed by an anonymous body-size limit - is not described, and the advisory explicitly rules out payment forgery.
judgements.what_would_settle_it: Whether the finding's 'no middleware at all' claim is meant to include a body-size limiter; as written it argues request-rate and method, not body size.

judgements.reason: Upstream safety filtering disabled by default for Gemini and Cohere. Configuration default with operator-policy consequence; unrelated defect.
World-writable log directory (0777) enabling audit-trail destruction and symlink swaps. Filesystem permission mechanism, local attacker; not the unauthenticated oversized-body memory/disk exhaustion.
SESSION_SECRET placeholder guard unreachable when unset and CryptoSecret reusing the same key -> session forgery. Different file and defect.
Unauthenticated /api/setup lacking CriticalRateLimit and TurnstileCheck, with GET /api/setup as an initialization oracle. Privilege-bootstrap defect on a different route.
0777 log directory plus a Stat probe that fails open. Permission and robustness defect on the log path; not full-body logging of anonymous requests.
/api/models and /api/models/ carrying different authorization levels one character apart. Routing/authorization confusion; unrelated.
TLS_INSECURE_SKIP_VERIFY applied process-wide via http.DefaultTransport. Different file, mechanism and consequence.
